C1 extension

C1 Technical Layer

Go beyond the learner-friendly overview and look at how acid structure, phenolic extraction, aroma chemistry, oxygen management, and elevage decisions shape the same grape into very different wines.

C1 technical layer

C1 Technical Layer

Go beyond the learner-friendly overview and look at how acid structure, phenolic extraction, aroma chemistry, oxygen management, and elevage decisions shape the same grape into very different wines.

Acid matrix and perceived freshness

Wine acidity is not just one number. Tartaric acid gives a stable backbone, malic acid adds a sharper green-apple edge, and pH changes how firm or soft that acidity feels in the glass.

Two wines can show similar total acidity but feel very different because pH, alcohol, fruit ripeness, and residual sugar change the final perception.

Phenolic extraction and tactile structure

Phenolic compounds come from grape skins, seeds, and sometimes stems. Extraction level depends on ripeness, temperature, cap management, and time on skins.

This is one reason texture can move from fine and chalky to coarse and drying even before oak influence is considered.

Ester formation and aroma expression

Yeast metabolism creates esters and other volatile compounds during fermentation. Their expression changes with strain choice, nutrient status, temperature, and later oxygen exposure.

Fruit aroma is not only a grape property. Fermentation conditions can amplify, mute, or redirect what the drinker smells.

Lees contact and autolytic texture

When wine stays on lees, yeast breakdown products can add creaminess, breadth, and more stable aromatic complexity.

A wine can feel fuller and more layered without becoming obviously oaky, which is important when learners compare stainless-steel and barrel-aged styles.

Oxidative versus reductive handling

Some winemaking styles protect the wine strongly from oxygen, while others allow controlled oxygen contact through barrel ageing, lees work, or cellar handling.

That choice changes aroma profile, texture, ageing path, and how quickly a wine moves from bright and tense to softer and more developed.

Cool-climate vs warm-climate Chardonnay

Cool-climate profile

Higher natural acidity, tighter fruit profile, more linear structure, and a greater chance that the wine reads as mineral or saline rather than broad.

Warm-climate profile

Riper fruit, higher alcohol risk, softer acid impression, and a broader mid-palate that can seem richer even before oak or malolactic influence is added.

Takeaway: Climate does not replace winemaking decisions, but it sets the structural starting point from which those decisions operate.

Stainless-steel ageing vs oak elevage

Stainless-steel handling

Usually aims to preserve primary fruit, cleaner reductive aromatics, and a more direct acid line.

Oak elevage

Can introduce oxygen exchange, spice or toast notes, tannin contribution, and a broader textural frame, especially when paired with lees work.

Takeaway: Oak is not just flavour. It is a structural tool that changes oxygen exposure and mouthfeel as well as aroma.

Short skin contact vs extended extraction

Short extraction

Lower phenolic pickup, softer tactile grip, and a cleaner fruit-forward style.

Extended extraction

More tannin and structural grip, higher bitterness risk, and greater demand for fruit concentration and balance.

Takeaway: Extraction decisions can sharpen or distort style depending on whether fruit weight is strong enough to carry the structure.

malolactic texture shift

malic acid -> malolactic conversion -> lactic acid -> lower sharpness -> rounder mouthfeel

The key effect is not only a chemical swap but a sensory shift: the wine usually feels less angular and more integrated on the palate.

fermentation aroma pathway

yeast strain -> fermentation temperature -> ester formation -> aroma profile -> perceived freshness or richness

A cooler and more protective fermentation can preserve lifted fruit notes, while warmer or less protected conditions can push the profile toward riper or broader aromas.

structure building pathway

ripeness -> phenolic extraction -> tannin quality -> texture -> finish length

Texture is not one isolated sensation. It reflects how grape maturity and extraction choices interact from the first sip to the final aftertaste.

C1 analysis prompts

  • If two Chardonnays show similar fruit notes but very different texture, which variables would you test first: malolactic conversion, lees contact, oak elevage, or climate? Why?
  • How would you distinguish acid-driven freshness from oak-driven roundness in a blind tasting note without reducing the explanation to simple like-or-dislike language?
  • Why is pH a useful idea for advanced learners even if they are not reading laboratory reports directly?
  • When a wine feels broad but not sweet, how can alcohol, glycerol, lees work, and acidity together explain that impression?

Step: Concept review

Technical Concepts

Start with the core ideas before opening the full concept map.

Acidity

The fresh, sour quality that gives wine energy and shape.

It helps a wine feel lively instead of flat.

Malic acid and lactic acid

Malic acid is sharp and green-apple-like; lactic acid is softer and rounder.

This contrast explains why some wines feel crisp while others feel creamy.

Fermentation

The process in which yeast changes grape sugar into alcohol and aroma compounds.

It shapes both flavour and texture, not only alcohol level.

Oak and oxygen

Barrel contact and controlled oxygen exposure can add flavour and soften structure.

These winemaking choices can change the final style even with the same grape.

Scenario: A learner compares two Chardonnays, one from a cool region and one from a warmer region.

Analysis: The cooler wine is likely to keep higher acidity and a sharper profile, while the warmer wine may feel fuller and riper. Malolactic conversion or oak aging can make the warmer style feel even softer and creamier.

Takeaway: Do not judge a wine only by grape name. Region and winemaking choices change the result.

Discussion

Open question 1 · opinion

Why is it too simple to say that one grape always makes one flavour?

Follow up: Which factor in the paragraph do you think changes the taste the most: climate, fermentation, or aging? Why?

Open question 2 · opinion

Do you think acidity or aroma gives better clues about a wine’s style first?

Follow up: If you were tasting a new wine, which one would you notice before the other, and what would that tell you?

Open question 3 · personal_experience

Have you ever tasted two drinks or foods made from the same ingredient but with very different results?

Follow up: What changed the most in that example: the place, the temperature, or the way it was made?

Open question 4 · comparison

How is a cool wine region different from a warm wine region in the way the wine tastes?

Follow up: Would you expect the cool-region wine to feel lighter or fuller than the warm-region wine? Why?

Key Concepts

Acidity

The fresh, sour quality that gives wine energy and shape.

It helps a wine feel lively instead of flat.

Malic acid and lactic acid

Malic acid is sharp and green-apple-like; lactic acid is softer and rounder.

This contrast explains why some wines feel crisp while others feel creamy.

Fermentation

The process in which yeast changes grape sugar into alcohol and aroma compounds.

It shapes both flavour and texture, not only alcohol level.

Oak and oxygen

Barrel contact and controlled oxygen exposure can add flavour and soften structure.

These winemaking choices can change the final style even with the same grape.

Tasting structure

A practical order for noticing acidity, texture, body, aroma, and winemaking clues.

It gives learners a repeatable method for understanding a glass of wine.

malolactic softening

malic acid -> malolactic conversion -> lactic acid -> rounder texture

When malic acid changes into lactic acid, the wine usually feels less sharp and more rounded.

style building

climate -> ripeness -> acidity -> body -> final style

Climate affects ripeness and acidity, and that changes how light, fresh, or rich the wine feels.

winemaking influence

yeast -> fermentation temperature -> aroma compounds -> texture

Yeast activity and fermentation temperature help shape aroma and the mouthfeel of the wine.

Scenario:A learner compares two Chardonnays, one from a cool region and one from a warmer region.

Analysis:The cooler wine is likely to keep higher acidity and a sharper profile, while the warmer wine may feel fuller and riper. Malolactic conversion or oak aging can make the warmer style feel even softer and creamier.

Takeaway:Do not judge a wine only by grape name. Region and winemaking choices change the result.

More discussion

Open question 5 · opinion

Why does malolactic conversion make some Chardonnay taste creamier?

Follow up: How would the wine feel different if that conversion did not happen?

Open question 6 · opinion

What do you think is the most important decision in winemaking: harvest timing, fermentation, or oak aging?

Follow up: How would your choice change the wine’s acidity, body, or aroma?
